title: A Topology-Aware Quantum-Classical Framework for Multi-Target Active Debris Removal using Gaussian Boson Sampling
authors: Komal Pandya, Saiyam Sakhuja, Nagaraj Kattian
abstract: The continued growth of orbital debris threatens the safety and sustainability of near-Earth space, making Active Debris Removal (ADR) an important mitigation strategy. Selecting $k$ targets from $N$ candidates yields a combinatorial search space of size $\binom{N}{k}$, making joint target selection and mission sequencing computationally demanding. We present a topology-aware quantum-classical framework integrating orbital mechanics, weighted orbital-transfer graphs, Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS), and multi-objective evolutionary optimization. Seven target-prioritization strategies represent physical consequence, orbital persistence, conjunction risk, network centrality, community structure, inferred source families, and random selection. GBS generates candidate target subsets from the weighted graph, which are then evaluated using PyGMO-based evolutionary optimization to identify servicing sequences that jointly minimize total velocity increment ($Δv$) and mission duration, accounting for modeled timing, propulsion, and mass feasibility. We evaluate the framework across three benchmark environments, SOCRATES Minefield, Collision Cloud, and Random, with candidate-pool sizes $N\in\{15,18,22,25\}$ and target cardinalities $k\in\{3,5\}$. The experiments characterize how benchmark topology, prioritization strategy, and problem scale relate to sampling behavior and downstream mission performance. By separating candidate-subset generation from detailed trajectory optimization, the framework offers a topology-aware approach to focusing computational effort on a limited set of candidate ADR missions.
summary: This paper proposes a novel quantum-classical framework to tackle the immense computational challenge of planning multi-target Active Debris Removal missions. It uses Gaussian Boson Sampling to intelligently sample promising subsets of debris targets from a weighted orbital graph. These subsets are then optimized classically to find the most efficient mission sequence, advancing the field of space sustainability.
main_problem: The combinatorial complexity of selecting and sequencing multiple targets for Active Debris Removal (ADR) in orbit is computationally prohibitive.
main_result: The proposed topology-aware quantum-classical framework successfully generates candidate target subsets using Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) before optimizing the mission sequence classically.
method: The framework combines graph theory to model orbital transfers, GBS for quantum-enhanced subset sampling, and multi-objective evolutionary optimization (PyGMO) to minimize mission $\Delta v$ and duration.
model_or_system: The system is the near-Earth space environment containing orbital debris, modeled as a weighted orbital-transfer graph. The core computational model is the hybrid quantum-classical pipeline.
key_observables: Hazard Removal Efficiency (HRE), Risk Capture Ratio (RCR), $\Delta v$, Mission Duration, Hafnian Concentration Ratio (HCR), and Graph Conductance (Cond).
important_parameters: Candidate pool sizes ($N\in\{15,18,22,25\}$) and target cardinalities ($k\in\{3,5\}$); orbital mechanics parameters.
main_assumptions: The problem is decomposed into two stages: quantum-guided subset discovery, followed by classical multi-objective optimization.
figures_summary: The notes mention figures showing object distributions across orbital regimes and historical launch volume, though the specific figure content for this paper is not detailed.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the ADR challenge, details the hybrid framework integrating orbital mechanics, graph theory, GBS, and multi-objective optimization, and evaluates it across benchmark environments using various diagnostic metrics.
why_interesting: It demonstrates a concrete application of quantum sampling (GBS) to a complex, real-world optimization problem in orbital mechanics, bridging quantum computation with classical astrodynamics.

Figure 5: Conceptual workflow of Gaussian Boson Sampling for a weighted graph. The symmetric graph matrix is factorized using the Autonne-Takagi decomposition, with the singular values determining the squeezing parameters and the unitary factor defining the linear optical transformation. Photon-number-resolving (PNR) detection produces photon-count patterns whose probabilities are governed by Hafnian-dependent expressions. The illustrative four-node graph continues the numerical example introduced in the text and shows one possible sampled pattern.
